# Network Reconnaissance

The information-gathering phase that precedes any assessment. Labs 10–12 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] walk it in the order it is actually performed: passive
collection first, active enumeration second, and only then anything that touches a service.

## Passive versus active — a real distinction with a real consequence

**Passive** collection introduces no traffic to the target. It queries third parties: `whois`, DNS
(`dig`, `host`, `dnsenum`, `fierce`), search-engine operators, certificate transparency, breach
corpora, and the internet-wide scanners (Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye) that already scanned everything.
Because the traffic goes to a third party, **nothing appears in the target's logs.**

**Active** enumeration sends packets to the target and gets both better data and a record of your
presence. Everything [[nmap]] does is active.

The consequence is a sequencing rule rather than a preference: exhaust passive sources first, because
each active probe spends detectability you cannot get back.

## What passive collection yields

Hostnames and subdomains, IP ranges and hosting provider, mail and nameserver configuration, DNSSEC
presence, exposed documents and their metadata, staff names and email format, technology stack from
public fingerprints, and known CVEs for anything identified (via NVD).

The lab's framing of *why* the people-oriented half matters is the durable point: OSINT is used to
optimise attacks against specific users. Dates, workplaces, schools and relatives feed password
guessing and pretexting, because human-chosen secrets correlate with human-knowable facts. The report
quotes Kaufman/Perlman/Speciner — "Humans are incapable of securely storing high-quality cryptographic
keys" — which is the honest statement of the problem: recon against people is effective because the
credential *is* a person-shaped secret.

DNS delegation tracing is the clean technical example — walking from the root servers down through
each delegation to the target's own nameservers, reading DS and RRSIG records along the way to see
where DNSSEC is in force. Entirely public infrastructure, zero contact with the target.

## What active enumeration adds

Host discovery, open/closed/filtered port state, service and version identification, OS fingerprinting
and network path. [[nmap]] recognises six port states, and the three ambiguous ones —
`filtered`, `open|filtered`, `closed|filtered` — carry most of the information: they tell you a
**packet filter** is present, which is a finding about the defence rather than about the service.

Two trade-offs the lab records:

- **Speed against stealth.** Timing templates run from paranoid to insane. Results in seconds generate
  traffic that is trivial to notice; results that are practically undetectable take weeks.
- **Scan type against what you learn.** Different TCP flag combinations (connect, SYN, null, FIN,
  ACK, window) elicit different responses from different stacks and filters — the point of running
  several is that the *differences* between their answers characterise the firewall.

Fragmentation, decoys and timing manipulation are covered as firewall/IDS evasion. Described here as a
category only.

## Recon is the input to everything after it

Lab 12 makes the pipeline explicit: enumerate services and versions, look up known vulnerabilities for
the exact versions found, then attempt exploitation with [[metasploit]] against deliberately
vulnerable hosts. This wiki records that the chain **was attempted and partly failed** — the report
ends with an exploit that connects but yields nothing — and describes no exploitation step, payload or
privilege-escalation procedure. See [[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]].

The defensive reading of the same material is the more useful one: every version string an active
scan can read is a version string an attacker can look up. Suppressing service banners, filtering
aggressively, and monitoring for scan patterns are all direct responses to what this phase collects.

## Legality is part of the technique

The lab material states it plainly: scanning is regulated differently in different jurisdictions, and
in some, running a scanner against infrastructure you do not own is an offence regardless of intent.
All work here was 2022 coursework against lab targets provided for the purpose.
